title: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
summary: Moving live data to a new store with no downtime: the four phases, why dual writes diverge, backfills that never overwrite newer data, verifying reads in production, and cutting over safely.
outcomes: Explain the four migration phases and why each one stays reversible until old data is deleted
Explain how dual writes diverge through races and partial failures, and how CDC or a single source of truth contains it
Design a backfill that never overwrites newer writes, and trace DBLog's watermark algorithm on a chunk
Compute how many compared reads are needed to catch a mismatch rate with a given confidence
Choose between application dual writes, triggers and log-based copying, and explain why cut-over must drain lag

lessons.title: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases

blocks.md:
Sooner or later a data model stops fitting the product. At Stripe, each Customer record once held at most one subscription inline; when customers needed many subscriptions, the field became an array, and every subscription change meant rewriting the whole Customer record. The fix was to move subscriptions into their own table. There were hundreds of millions of Subscription objects, and the API had to stay up and correct the whole time.

An **online data migration** moves live data from an old store (a table, schema or database) to a new one while the service keeps serving traffic, with no maintenance window.

Stripe's post names three things that make this hard:

- **Scale**: touching every object is real work for the production database.
- **Uptime**: Stripe performs infrastructure upgrades online, so the service could not be paused.
- **Accuracy**: the data was used across thousands of lines of code, and changing them all at once would miss edge cases.

Each naive plan breaks one of these. A maintenance window breaks uptime. A single big-bang code change breaks accuracy. A simple sequential copy breaks on scale: Stripe's own illustration is that at one second per object, migrating one hundred million objects in sequence takes over three years.

blocks.caption: Copy time for N objects at t seconds each with P parallel workers. Lesson 3 uses the same model for the backfill.

blocks.md:
The standard answer is the **four-phase dual-write pattern** that Stripe describes:

1. **Dual write**: write every change to both the old and the new store, then **backfill** (copy) the existing objects so both hold the same data.
2. **Move reads**: change every read path to read from the new store.
3. **Move writes**: change every write path to write the new store (Stripe kept archiving to the old one).
4. **Remove old data**: stop writing the old store and delete the old data and code.

A **read path** is any code that loads the data; a **write path** is any code that changes it. The **source of truth** is the store whose value wins when the two disagree.

blocks.prompt: Why not do phases 2 and 3 at the same time: switch reads and writes to the new store in one deploy?
blocks.reveal:
Because then nothing is left to fall back on. While reads move (phase 2), writes still go to **both** stores, so the old store stays complete and up to date. If the new read path returns wrong answers, you flip reads back and lose nothing.

Switching writes at the same moment would make the old store stale from the first request. Any bug found afterwards would need a reverse migration instead of a flag flip. Splitting the phases means each step changes one thing and each step can be undone.

blocks.title: The four phases, one store at a time

scenes.caption: Before the migration: every write and every read uses the old store. The new table exists but is empty and unused.
Phase 1, dual write: every write now also goes to the new store. New objects appear in both, but objects created earlier exist only in the old store.
Still phase 1, backfill: an offline job over a database snapshot lists the IDs still missing, and a fleet of workers copies them into the new store.
Phase 2, move reads: reads switch to the new store, verified first by comparing both answers in production. Writes still go to both, so switching back is a flag flip.
Phase 3, move writes: code paths are refactored one at a time to write the new store first and then archive to the old one. The new store becomes the source of truth.
Phase 4, remove old data: writes to the old store stop and the old field is deleted. Only now is rolling back no longer a flag flip.

blocks.md: Until phase 4, at least one store is complete and current, and the other one is being kept in step with it. That is what makes every earlier step reversible. Plan each phase so it can be rolled out gradually (by percentage of objects or code paths) and rolled back with a flag.

Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

blocks.question: Dual writes have been on for a week, but the backfill has not run. A read from the new Subscriptions table for a customer who subscribed two years ago and has not changed since returns nothing. What happened?
options: The dual write to the new table failed for this customer
Nothing went wrong: untouched old objects only reach the new store through the backfill
The new table needs a read replica before it can serve reads
Dual writes copy old rows lazily on the first read, so the next read will succeed
blocks.explain: Dual writes only cover writes made after they were turned on. Stripe also copied objects lazily whenever they were *updated*, but an object nobody touches is copied only by the backfill. This is why reads must not move until the backfill and a completeness check are done.

blocks.question: Which step is the real point of no return, where undoing it needs more than flipping a flag back?
options: Starting dual writes
Switching reads to the new store
Switching writes to the new store while still archiving to the old one
Stopping writes to the old store and deleting its data
blocks.explain: As long as some code keeps the old store current (dual writes in phases 1 to 3, archiving in phase 3), you can point traffic back at it. Once old writes stop and its data is deleted, going back would mean a new migration in the other direction.

lessons.title: How dual writes silently diverge, and how to contain it

blocks.md:
From the consistency models course: a single store can give every write one place in one order, so all readers agree on the latest value. Two separate stores give you two independent orders. A dual write is the application, not a database, trying to keep those two orders the same, and it has no way to do so.

Martin Kleppmann's essay on dual writes shows the two failure modes that follow: **race conditions** and **partial failures**.

blocks.title: Two clients dual-write the same key

scenes.caption: Client 1 sets X = A. It writes the old store first, as the dual-write code says.
Client 2 sets X = B. Its write to the old store lands after client 1's, so the old store ends at B.
Client 2 is faster on its second write: X = B reaches the new store first.
Client 1's delayed write arrives last. Every request succeeded, yet the old store holds B and the new store holds A, and they stay that way until X is written again.

blocks.prompt: In the scene above, every request returned success. How would you find out that X differs between the stores?
blocks.reveal:
Usually you would not, until something else breaks. No error was raised anywhere. Kleppmann's point is exactly this: the stores stay inconsistent until X is overwritten again, and you may discover it months later with no trace of how it happened.

That is why a migration needs an **independent check** (lesson 4) and a **repair path** (the backfill), not just dual writes.

blocks.md: How often does the race bite? Take a deliberately simple model: two clients each write the old store then the new store, and the four writes happen in some global order. There are $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ such orders. A short script enumerates them and applies last-writer-wins at each store.

blocks.title: All six orders of four writes (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Columns 1 to 6 are the six global orders: A1A2B1B2, A1B1A2B2, A1B1B2A2, B1A1A2B2, B1A1B2A2, B1B2A1A2. A1 and A2 are client 1's writes to old then new; B1 and B2 are client 2's.
Each store keeps the last value it received. Old store: whichever of A1 and B1 came later. New store: whichever of A2 and B2 came later.
Orders 3 and 4 leave the stores different: the clients' writes are ordered one way at the old store and the other way at the new store.

blocks.md:
In this toy model 2 of 6 orders diverge. Real rates depend on how often the same key is written concurrently and how much the two write latencies vary, so do not read 1 in 3 as a prediction. The lesson is that **any** overlap between two writers to one key can produce it.

The second failure mode needs no concurrency at all. The write to the old store commits, then the write to the new store fails: a timeout, a crash, a deploy that kills the process. Worse, a timeout is ambiguous: the new store may or may not have applied the write. Without a transaction spanning both stores, one side can be left behind.

Migrations still use dual writes, so the job is to contain these failures:

- **Pick one source of truth per phase.** In phase 1 the old store is authoritative. A failed write to the new store is logged and repaired later, not shown to the user.
- **Copy whole objects, not deltas.** Rewriting the full current object is idempotent: running it twice or late does no harm. Stripe also copied existing objects lazily whenever they were updated.
- **Ramp up gradually.** Stripe raised the percentage of duplicated objects slowly while watching operational metrics, because the extra write adds load.
- **Rerun the backfill and keep comparing.** Drift that slips through is found by the completeness job and the read comparisons, then repaired.

blocks.title: Application dual writes vs one ordered log

scenes.caption: Application dual write: the app sends two independent writes. Nothing orders client 1's pair against client 2's pair, and either write can fail on its own.
Log-based alternative: the app writes only the old store. The database's transaction log already records every committed change in one order.
A change-data-capture (CDC) reader tails that log and applies changes to the new store in commit order. If it crashes, it resumes from its last log position.

blocks.md:
The structural fix is to stop making two independent writes. Kleppmann's answer is to put every write into one totally ordered, append-only log and have each store apply that log in order. A database already keeps such a log (the MySQL binlog, the PostgreSQL write-ahead log). **Change data capture (CDC)** reads it and replays changes elsewhere. Netflix's DBLog paper lists schema migration among the uses of its CDC framework.

When the app must also emit events, the **transactional outbox** pattern writes the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the data change, and a CDC connector such as Debezium's outbox event router publishes it.
Two independent writes have no shared order and no shared atomicity. Either keep one store authoritative and repair the other, or derive the second store from the first store's commit log.

blocks.question: A dual write does `old.increment(counter, 1)` then `new.increment(counter, 1)`, retrying the second call on timeout. After a week the new counters are slightly *higher* than the old ones. What is the most likely cause?
options: Clock skew between the two stores
A timed-out increment had actually been applied, so the retry applied it twice
The backfill copied counters that were already migrated
Last-writer-wins dropped some increments in the old store
blocks.explain: A timeout does not mean the write failed. Retrying a non-idempotent delta (add 1) after an ambiguous failure double-applies it. Writing the full current value read from the source of truth, or making the operation idempotent with a request ID, removes the problem.

blocks.question: Why does reading changes from the old store's transaction log remove the two-client race?
options: The log is stored on faster disks
The log batches writes, so they arrive together
The new store receives changes in the single order in which the old store committed them
CDC takes a lock on each row while it copies it
blocks.explain: The race happens because the two stores order the same writes differently. A log consumer replays one commit order, so the new store ends with the same last value as the old store for every key once it catches up.

lessons.title: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes

blocks.md:
Dual writes cover the future. The **backfill** covers the past: it copies every object that exists only in the old store. Stripe found that the costliest part was simply *finding* the objects to migrate, since scanning the production database would mean many expensive queries.

So they moved the search offline. Database snapshots were loaded into a Hadoop cluster, and a Scalding (a Scala library for MapReduce jobs) job listed every subscription ID that needed copying. A multi-threaded fleet of processes then copied those IDs in parallel. Finally they **ran the Scalding job again** to confirm that no subscription was missing from the new table.

blocks.title: Backfill wall-clock time vs number of workers

scenes.caption: 100 million objects at 1 s each. One worker needs 27,778 hours (3.17 years), Stripe's 'over three years'.
Time falls as 1/P: 100 workers take 277.8 hours, 1,000 take 27.8 hours. Simplified: real speedup stops when the database, not the workers, is the bottleneck.
Cheaper per-object work moves the whole line down. Drag both sliders: the knobs are fewer seconds per object and more workers, both bounded by production load.

blocks.md: Parallelism solves the time problem but creates a correctness problem. A backfill worker does *read old, then write new*, and those two steps are not atomic. Any dual write that lands on the same object between them is newer than what the worker is holding.

blocks.prompt: A backfill worker reads subscription S, then pauses for 50 ms. During the pause, the app dual-writes a change to S. What should the worker's write do?
blocks.reveal:
It must **not** replace the newer value. Anything the dual write put in the new store reflects a later state of S than the worker's copy.

The next figure shows the blind overwrite, and the simplest guard.

blocks.title: A backfill overwrites a newer value

scenes.caption: The backfill reads subscription S from the old store: plan = basic.
Before the worker writes, a user upgrades. The app dual-writes plan = pro to both stores.
The worker now writes the stale copy it read earlier. A blind overwrite replaces pro with basic in the new store.
With insert-if-absent instead, the write finds S already present (the dual write put it there) and does nothing. The newer value survives.

blocks.md:
Three ways to make a backfill write safe:

- **Insert if absent.** If the row is already in the new store, some newer write put it there, so skip it. GitHub's gh-ost schema change tool copies rows into its new (ghost) table with `INSERT IGNORE ... SELECT`, so the row copy never overwrites a row that the change stream already applied.
- **Version check.** Keep a version number or update counter on each object and write only if the incoming version is higher (a conditional or compare-and-set write).
- **Order against the log.** If the new store is fed from the old store's change log, interleave the backfill with that log so a copied row can never land after a newer event for the same key. That is DBLog's watermark algorithm, next.

blocks.question: A backfill uses insert-if-absent. A user deletes subscription S: the dual write deletes it from both stores. A backfill worker had read S from the old store just before the delete, and writes it to the new store just after. What happens?
options: S comes back to life in the new store, because after the delete there is no row to block the insert
Nothing: insert-if-absent skips S because it already exists
The insert fails with a foreign-key error
The old store also gets S back
blocks.explain: Insert-if-absent treats a missing row as never copied, but here it is missing because it was deleted. The fix is to remember deletes (a tombstone row or a version that marks deletion), or to order the copy against the change log so the delete is applied after the copied row.

blocks.md:
Netflix's **DBLog** (Andreakis and Papapanagiotou, 2020) captures a table's full state while it keeps streaming changes from the transaction log, without locks and without stalling the log for long. It selects rows in primary-key chunks and brackets each select with two **watermarks**: single-row updates to a dedicated watermark table, which show up in the change log.

The select ran somewhere between the low and the high watermark, but the exact position is unknown. So any chunk row whose key also appears in the log *inside the window* is dropped from the chunk; the log event, which is at least as new, wins. The remaining chunk rows are emitted at the high watermark, before any later log event. For this to work the database must emit changes in commit order and the select must see everything committed before it runs (the paper calls these non-stale reads).

blocks.title: DBLog watermark chunk selection on keys k1 to k6

scenes.caption: Steps 1 and 2: pause log processing and write a low watermark (a UUID update to a watermark table). It appears in the change log like any other row change.
Step 3: select the next chunk by primary key. The values are whatever was committed when the select ran, at some unknown point after the low watermark.
Steps 4 and 5: write a high watermark and resume reading the log. Between the two watermarks the log shows updates to k2 (now 21) and k4 (now 41).
Step 6: inside the window, every key that has a log event is dropped from the chunk, because we cannot tell whether the select saw the old or the new value. Log events go out as they arrive.
Step 7: at the high watermark, the remaining chunk rows k1, k3, k5, k6 are emitted. Every key now has its latest value and no old row overwrote a newer event.

blocks.caption: DBLog Algorithm 1, condensed from the paper (pseudocode).
blocks.code:
pause log processing
lw, hw = uuid(), uuid()
update watermark_table set value = lw        # low watermark
chunk = select next chunk by primary key     # pk index scan with a LIMIT
update watermark_table set value = hw        # high watermark
resume log processing

in_window = False
for e in change_log:
    if e is watermark(lw): in_window = True
    elif e is watermark(hw):
        emit_all(chunk)                      # rows not touched in window
        in_window = False
    else:
        if in_window and e.key in chunk:
            chunk.remove(e.key)              # log event is newer: drop row
        emit(e)

blocks.md: Debezium's incremental snapshots work the same way: they sort each table by primary key, read it in chunks (1,024 rows by default), and use a snapshot window to drop buffered snapshot rows that collide with streamed events for the same key. Progress is tracked, so an interrupted snapshot resumes where it stopped instead of starting over.

A backfill copy is always an *old* view of a row. Whatever mechanism you use (insert-if-absent, versions, or watermarks), it must guarantee that a backfilled row can never land after a newer write for the same key, and that deletes are remembered.

blocks.question: In DBLog, why drop a chunk row whose key changed inside the window, rather than keep the chunk's value?
options: The chunk value is always older than the log event
The select's exact log position is unknown, so its value may be older than the event; the event is at least as new, so emitting it alone is always safe
Dropping rows makes chunks smaller and faster to emit
Log events contain more columns than chunk rows
blocks.explain: The select happened somewhere inside the window, so for a key changed in the window it may have read the value before or after that change. Keeping the log event, which is the latest committed change for that key up to that point, is correct either way; keeping the chunk row could reintroduce an older value.

lessons.title: Proving the new read path before trusting it

blocks.md:
Once the stores are in sync, phase 2 moves reads to the new store. Stripe did not trust the backfill blindly: they used GitHub's **Scientist** library to read from both tables in production and alert when the results differed. Only after everything matched did they switch reads.

Scientist calls the existing code the **control** (a `use` block) and the new code the **candidate** (a `try` block). Running the two side by side on real traffic is often called a *shadow read*.

blocks.caption: Illustrative Scientist experiment for this migration (Ruby). The compare block decides what counts as equal. With the default experiment class the candidate never runs: define your own class with enabled? and publish first.
blocks.code:
require "scientist"

class SubscriptionReader
  include Scientist

  def for_customer(customer)
    science "subscriptions-read-path" do |e|
      e.use { customer.subscriptions }                         # old store
      e.try { Subscription.where(customer_id: customer.id).to_a } # new store
      e.compare { |control, candidate| control.map(&:id).sort == candidate.map(&:id).sort }
    end # always returns the control value
  end
end

blocks.title: One read inside a Scientist experiment

scenes.caption: The read path calls the experiment. `enabled?` (for example a percentage) and `run_if` decide whether the candidate runs at all this time.
Both blocks run, in random order, and each one is timed. The `use` block reads the old store; the `try` block reads the new store.
The results differ, so the experiment publishes a mismatch with both values for an engineer to inspect.
The caller always gets the control value. Users never see the candidate's answer, and a candidate exception is recorded, not raised.

blocks.md:
According to the Scientist README, `run` decides whether to run the candidate, randomizes the order of the two blocks, measures their wall and CPU time, compares the results (with `==` unless you give a `compare` block), swallows and records exceptions from the candidate, and publishes everything. It **always returns the control value**.

Three knobs matter during a migration:

- `enabled?` on your experiment class decides how often the experiment runs; the README's example is a percentage check. Ramp it up gradually, because the candidate adds load and latency.
- `run_if` disables the experiment for some requests, such as non-staff users.
- `ignore` blocks mark known, understood mismatches so they do not drown real ones.

Scientist is for code that only reads. Its README says that because the candidate may or may not run, it is only safe for wrapping methods that do not change data. Write paths need different checks, such as comparing stored rows after the fact.
How much comparison is enough? If each read independently has probability $p$ of exposing a bug, the chance of seeing at least one mismatch in $n$ compared reads is:

blocks.caption: Simple model: independent reads, a fixed bug rate. Real bugs cluster on rare object shapes, which makes them harder to hit, not easier.

blocks.title: Chance of seeing at least one mismatch

scenes.caption: If 1 read in 100,000 disagrees, 20,000 clean comparisons are weak evidence: you would see no mismatch 81.9 percent of the time.
You need about 299,572 compared reads to see a 1e-5 bug with 95 percent probability (n = ln 0.05 / ln(1 - p)).
Every factor of 10 rarer needs 10 times more comparisons. Drag p: rare bugs are exactly the ones a short experiment misses. Simplified: assumes independent reads.

blocks.md: Turn that into a schedule. Suppose (a stated example, not Stripe's numbers) the read path serves 2,000 reads per second and the experiment runs on 1 percent of them. That is 1,728,000 compared reads per day, so a bug with $p = 10^{-5}$ would show up about 17 times a day, and you would be nearly certain to see it within a day. At the same rate, a quiet hour proves much less.

Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.
Switch reads only when sustained, high-volume comparison shows zero unexplained mismatches, and keep dual writes running so the switch can be undone by a flag.

blocks.question: An experiment compared 20,000 reads with zero mismatches. The new path actually returns wrong data on 1 read in 100,000. How likely was this clean result?
options: About 1.8 percent
About 18 percent
About 50 percent
About 82 percent
blocks.explain: The probability of no mismatch is (1 - 0.00001) to the power 20,000, which is about 0.819. A clean run that short says little about rare bugs; you need roughly 300,000 comparisons for 95 percent confidence at this rate.

blocks.question: The candidate block raises an exception on 2 percent of reads during the experiment. What do users see?
options: Errors on 2 percent of requests
Errors only when the experiment is enabled
The normal control result; the exceptions are recorded as mismatches for engineers
A retry against the old store after a delay
blocks.explain: Scientist swallows and records exceptions raised in the try block and returns the control value. The README does warn that it does not protect against candidate timeouts, so slow candidates can still hurt users.

lessons.title: Flipping writes, cutting over and deleting the old path

blocks.md:
Phase 3 reverses the direction of the copy. Until now, data was written to the old store and copied to the new one. Stripe changed each write path to **write the new store first and then archive to the old one**, keeping the two consistent at every step so each change could be watched.

Stripe called this refactor arguably the hardest part: subscription logic (updates, prorations, renewals) spanned thousands of lines across multiple services. They split it into the smallest code paths they could, never changed more than a few hundred lines at once, and ran more Scientist experiments along the way.

blocks.caption: From Stripe's post: once every path was moved, any remaining use of the old field fails loudly.
blocks.code:
class Customer
  def subscriptions
    Opus::Error.hard("Accessing subscriptions array on customer")
  end
end

blocks.md: Phase 4 removes the old path. When no code reads the old `subscriptions` field, the archive write is deleted and the new table becomes the only source of truth. Old data is removed the same way it was copied: lazily first (Stripe emptied the array whenever a subscription was loaded), then with a final Scalding job and migration that found every object still holding old data.

blocks.title: Where rollback is a flag flip (illustrative, no real durations)

scenes.caption: Phase 1: dual writes ramp up, then the backfill runs and the completeness job is rerun. Reads still use the old store.
Phase 2: comparisons run, then reads move to the new store. Both stores still receive every write, so moving reads back is safe.
Phase 3: write paths flip one by one to new first, then archive to old. The old store is still current, so a broken path can be flipped back.
Phase 4: old writes stop and old data is deleted lazily, then by a final job. From the marker on, there is no cheap way back.

blocks.md:
The same pattern shrinks to a single table when you change its schema in place, which is what online schema change tools do. GitHub's **gh-ost** creates an empty *ghost* table with the new schema, copies rows over in chunks along a unique key, and at the same time reads the MySQL binary log as if it were a replica, applying every change to the original table onto the ghost table. It needs no triggers, and it can throttle, pausing all of its writes, when replication lag or load gets high.

Older tools used triggers instead. pt-online-schema-change adds `AFTER INSERT`, `AFTER UPDATE` and `AFTER DELETE` triggers that apply each change to the new table in the same transaction: a synchronous dual write done by the database.

blocks.prompt: gh-ost has locked the original table for writes. Why can it not run the rename to the ghost table right away?
blocks.reveal:
Because the copy is **asynchronous**: changes reach the ghost table through the binary log, so at the moment of locking there are still events in the pipeline that have not been applied. Swapping now would serve a table missing the last writes.

gh-ost first drains that backlog while writes are blocked, then performs an atomic rename. Its cut-over is built so that if a connection dies or a timeout fires, the rename does not happen and everything returns to the state before cut-over.

blocks.title: gh-ost style cut-over: lock, drain, swap (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Before cut-over the applier trails the binary log. In this model it has 2,000 events left to apply when the cut-over starts at t = 100 ms.
The original table is locked for writes, so the backlog stops growing. Writes queue up and wait.
At 10,000 events per second the backlog drains in 2,000 / 10,000 s = 200 ms. Only then is the ghost table complete.
The atomic rename swaps the ghost table in and blocked writes proceed against it. If anything times out instead, the lock is released and the original stays in place.

blocks.md:
gh-ost's docs also show how to build trust in the copy itself: GitHub continuously ran "trivial" migrations (no real column change) on production replicas, stopped replication, cut over and back, and compared checksums of the original and ghost tables, expecting zero failures. That is the write-side counterpart of the read comparisons in lesson 4.

Choosing a mechanism:

- **Application dual writes**: work across any two stores and any data model change, but you own the races, partial failures and repair.
- **Triggers in the same database**: atomic with the original write, but add load and lock contention to every write on a hot table.
- **Log-based copy (gh-ost, CDC, DBLog)**: one commit order and pausable, but asynchronous, so a cut-over must drain the lag.

Common failure modes: a write path nobody knew about keeps writing only the old store (find it with loud errors and comparisons); deletes resurrected by the backfill; reads switched before the completeness job is rerun; and deleting old data before every reader of the old field is gone.
Move one thing at a time, keep one store complete until the very end, and measure agreement continuously. The deletion in phase 4 is the only step that should be hard to undo.

blocks.question: Midway through phase 3, the new write path for prorations is found to compute the wrong amount. Most other paths already write the new store first and archive to the old one. What is the safest response?
options: Restore the new store from last night's backup
Pause all writes until the bug is fixed
Delete the old store so the two cannot disagree
Flip the prorations path back to the old write order; the old store is still current because every path still writes it
blocks.explain: In phase 3 every write still reaches the old store (as the primary or as an archive), so it is complete. Rolling one path back by a flag is cheap. That safety disappears in phase 4, which is why it comes last.

blocks.question: A gh-ost migration's applier is 6,000 events behind and applies 10,000 events per second. Using the simplified model, roughly how long are writes blocked during cut-over?
options: About 6 ms
About 60 ms
About 600 ms
About 6 seconds
blocks.explain: 6,000 events at 10,000 events per second take 0.6 s. That is why tools throttle and wait for lag to be small before cutting over: the write pause grows with the backlog.
